The CEO of Ticketmaster/Live Nation just finished testifying.
If you remember, last week I told you that our antitrust case against them had hit a rough patch.
The USDOJ, which had been leading the case alongside 40 state AGs, suddenly cut a cheap deal behind closed doors and bailed.
On their way out the door, they said we could join their deal if we wanted. I declined. So did the vast majority of the other AGs. We told Ticketmaster we'd see them back in court, and the trial resumed a few days later. It's still going on, and I'll report back on it soon.
### Nexstar + Tegna = Largest TV Company Ever
Now from one antitrust case to another.
We started this case last week. My bet is you haven't heard about it, but it's a big one.
Here's the situation:
The biggest TV company in the country is trying to buy one of its biggest competitors. If it does, it's going to raise prices, downsize a lot of local news, and control a huge chunk of the news our country sees every day.
The big company here is called Nexstar. You probably haven't heard of it, but it owns about 200 stations, including Fox, ABC, CBS, and NBC stations all across the country.
The second biggest TV company is Sinclair. It's got about 180 stations.
The third biggest is Tegna, and that's the one Nexstar is trying to buy. If it does, it will become the biggest TV company in American history and will reach 80% of American homes.
No single company has ever controlled that much of American broadcast television, and North Carolina would be the second-most impacted state in the country, especially in Charlotte, Greensboro, and our northeastern counties.
Take a look:
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/69fc3ca2-0993-424d-ac6d-2a7756171d84?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Why does this matter?
Say Nexstar owns both the Fox and CBS stations where you live. Now they can go to your cable company and say, "Pay our new price or we pull both channels." Your cable company is going to pay. And you're going to see it on your next bill.
Nexstar knows that once it buys out one of its biggest competitors, if you want to watch local news or football on the weekend, you're going to have to pay more.
Nexstar has already told its investors that if this deal goes through, it's going to make $135m by raising prices and another $165m by finding "synergies," which is another way of saying, "laying off local reporters."
Higher bills are not the only consequence. When Nexstar buys a competitor in the same city, it "consolidates" the newsrooms, effectively removing one of them. The company has an internal name for this: the "Consolidation Playbook."
In Indianapolis, for example, Nexstar owns both the FOX and CBS affiliates. Two stations that are supposedly competitors now share the same anchors, the same reporting team, the same news director, and the same website.
If all this sounds like it should trigger some antitrust laws, _it does._
The federal government has a standard index to measure whether a merger concentrates too much power in one company. The USDOJ and the FTC have used it for decades. Courts rely on it.
When a merger pushes concentration past a certain threshold and increases it by more than 100 points, it's presumed illegal. In every single NC market affected by this deal, the merger doesn't just cross the legal threshold, _it obliterates it._
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/1f19f73a-5727-4057-842b-bcf8bc8fce54?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
So last week, I joined a number of AGs and we filed a lawsuit to block the merger.
**Then things took a quick turn.**
As soon as we filed, Nexstar hit the gas to try to close the deal before a court could stop them.
It was remarkable. Less than 24 hours after we filed our lawsuit, the FCC, which would normally block a merger like this, suddenly waived its rules and let it happen. Then the USDOJ reportedly dropped its investigation and basically said, "Go right ahead."
For all of that to happen in 24 hours is very strange. Now Nexstar is declaring victory and saying the deal is done.
_Not so fast._
We have now filed an emergency motion that basically says, "Hey judge, they're trying to get around you. They know the law is not on their side, and the last thing they want is for you to hear our case. _That 's exactly why you should._ Let's take a breath before they're allowed to walk off the field as the biggest TV company in American history. Let's see if these antitrust rules were written for a reason, because I bet they were."
We used more formal language than that, but that's the gist of it.
Our motion is pending right now. Will update you soon.
Best,
Jeff

permits, and rallying brand new first-time activists who are ready to make
history.

[ https://act.ourrevolution.com/go/34881?source=email-20260325&t=1112&akid=10433%2E5885482%2ES-iDWG ]Headline: 'No Kings' protests may draw biggest — and most diverse —
anti-Trump crowds ever

In Kansas, organizer Pam Martin told us: "Unfortunately in Kansas, all our
representatives and senators, except one, have rubber stamped every
lawless action taken by Trump. Raising our voices in events like No Kings
rallies is one of the strongest weapons we have to let our elected
officials know we are angry and that if they don't take us seriously they
risk losing their congressional seats."

Momentum is building: on the first No Kings Day in June, 5 million turned
out. By October, we grew to 7 million people in 2,700 towns and cities.
Now, we're racing to break our records – gaining ground with events deep
into what Trump *thought* was MAGA country.

But every single new rally takes resources – money for signs, permits,
training, legal aid, security, and mobilizing volunteers. If events are
underfunded, they shrink, or worse, never happen at all.

[ https://act.ourrevolution.com/go/34881?t=1106&amount=22&refcode=email-20260325nd&amounts=9%2C22%2C27%2C46%2C66&firstname=Peter%20Willis&lastname=&email=dpwillis67%40gmail.com&zip=18326&city=Cresco&state=PA&akid=10433%2E5885482%2ES-iDWG ]If you've ever wanted to plant a flag in the heart of Trump country and
show him that millions are saying "No Kings," this is your moment. Chip in
whatever you can to power No Kings Day on March 28 – and let's shatter
records.

Let’s make sure when history looks back at March 28, it sees a people –
urban and rural, blue state and red – united to say we will *never* accept
a king in America.

When we organize, we win.

A lot of people have been asking me about redistricting.

If we’re serious about protecting it, we cannot and will not just sit back and watch. Not in Virginia, not in Maryland, and not anywhere. The DMV can and must be a pillar of resistance against Trump’s power grab.
Early voting is already underway and April 21 is the final day for votes to come in. body:
# [](https://ginafortexas.com/?refcode=em_ms_gh_header)[](https://ginafortexas.com/?refcode=em_ms_gh_header)
Peter, something is happening across this country right now.
[](https://act.ginafortexas.com/go/1356?c0=em_ms_gh_20260325_1_maralago.y5tJft&refcode=em20260325-805&t=1&akid=805%2E299639%2EO8PhlI)
Last night, Democrats flipped seats in districts that nobody thought were in play — including a state house seat in a district where Donald Trump himself lives. Mar-a-Lago is in that district. The anger folks are feeling across the country has reached Trump’s backyard.
And it’s not just Florida. From coast to coast, voters are showing up and taking their communities back. And here in Texas, we didn’t need to see last night’s results to know the tide was turning.
A few weeks ago, union leader and veteran Taylor Rehmet won in Tarrant County — a seat that hadn’t gone our way in over 30 years, in a district Trump won by 17 points, while being outspent 10-to-1.
**That happened here. This is what’s possible when Texans have real resources behind them.**
[**Chip in $5 right now and let’s keep our momentum going >>**](https://act.ginafortexas.com/go/625?c0=em_ms_gh_20260325_1_maralago.PTssqb&refcode=em20260325-805&amount=5&t=2&akid=805%2E299639%2EO8PhlI)
The data show we’re just getting started. Gina is now **tied with Greg Abbott in TX-23** — a district he normally wins by double digits.
Texans aren’t waiting for someone else to save them. They’re already taking Texas back.
Greg Abbott has had years to deliver for working families. Instead, he’s delivered higher costs, failing schools, and a government that works for his billionaire donors — not for Texans. And we’re done with it.
Gina is running because Texas deserves a governor who actually shows up. And the numbers we’re seeing show that voters agree.
Abbott’s donors are watching these results too. They’re going to spend tens of millions of dollars to protect him. We need to be ready.
**[Chip in $5 right now to help take Texas back>>](https://act.ginafortexas.com/go/625?c0=em_ms_gh_20260325_1_maralago.PTssqb&refcode=em20260325-805&amount=5&t=3&akid=805%2E299639%2EO8PhlI)**

The momentum you’re seeing across the country is real. Texas is leading the way. Let’s get Gina over the finish line and give Texans the representation they deserve.
Thank you,
Team Gina

body:
All they’ve known over the last decade is the chaos, cruelty, and corruption of Donald Trump

Derek, I realized something the other day. I’ve got four kids (24, 21, 17, and 15) – and their entire frame of reference on politics, taking their dad out of it, has been shaped by Donald Trump. All my kids — and young people all across Pennsylvania — have known over the last decade is the chaos, cruelty, and corruption of Donald Trump. This brand of politics — it’s corrosive. It’s corrosive to our communities, where hard-working folks are sorted and divided into in-groups and out-groups. It’s corrosive to our kids when lying and cheating are rewarded by those in D.C. And Derek, it’s corrosive to the values our Commonwealth was founded on: Liberty, equality, tolerance, and freedom. **Our country is so much better than this. And we’re proving that every day here in Pennsylvania.** _We’ve pushed our differences aside. We’ve brought folks together. And Derek, we’ve gotten a lot of sh*t done because of it._ [_**But all of that progress? None of it was handed to us. We fought like hell for it in the last election — and now, we need to do it again. * * *
### The Chavez Reckoning
[The New York Times published what can only be described as a devastating, meticulously documented investigation into Cesar Chavez](https://substack.com/redirect/13b7d889-4533-462f-9af0-5a33a4e54f99?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), co-founder of the United Farm Workers, labor movement icon, and for millions of Mexican Americans, a figure of near-mythical stature.
Thanks for reading! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.
[Pledge your support](https://substack..lwIJ7vL54M383ei9x6ON7jOdk6atnPqe79KnPNm40yc?&utm_medium=email&utm_source=subscribe-widget-preamble&utm_content=192107444)
The allegations are serious. And the response from the UFW ([click here to view their online statement](https://substack.com/redirect/51c8cae6-73a9-4dc0-8ea5-0cab9a2a2882?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)) only adds weight to what is already an overwhelming evidentiary record.
We won't pretend this is easy to process.
For Chuck, who has spent his career as one of the country's few prominent Latino labor leaders, this is personal. For Mike, who grew up in the shadow of the UFW organizing drives in Ventura County, it cuts deep in a different way. But personal discomfort is not an excuse to look away.
What we're watching in real time is what happens when a community built its political identity around a single human being rather than a set of values and a movement. The statues, the schools, the holiday, the bust in the Oval Office. All of it now carries an asterisk. And the question before us isn't whether that asterisk exists. It's what we do next.
Here's our argument: the movement was always bigger than the man. [Dolores Huerta, 96 years old, co-founder, and herself a victim according to her own courageous statement](https://substack.com/redirect/6457fe5c-8c02-4890-bd3b-704fe38d43d8?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), represents what this fight was actually about. The farm workers who organized, who went on strike, who built collective power from nothing represent what this fight was actually about. That work doesn't disappear because its most famous face has been exposed as deeply, profoundly flawed.
But this moment also demands something of us politically. We have to stop deifying people. Full stop. The cult of personality is dangerous in every direction. Whether the idol is Cesar Chavez or Donald Trump. When we place human beings on marble pedestals, we make ourselves vulnerable to exactly this kind of collapse. The antidote isn't cynicism. It's investing in ideas, institutions, and movements. Not individual saviors.
* * *
### Illinois: $50 Million and Not One Dollar for Us
On the same day the Chavez story broke, [Illinois held its Democratic Senate primary](https://substack.com/redirect/06749d6f-bc40-46d5-aee5-bade6851628f?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), and the results handed us a perfect case study in exactly what's wrong with how both parties approach the Latino vote.
The race featured three well-funded candidates: Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi, Lt. Governor Juliana Stratton, and Congresswoman Robin Kelly. Combined hard money and outside spending topped $50 million. Governor Pritzker alone dropped $5 million into a super PAC backing Stratton.
Illinois has 1.1 million registered Latino voters. It is the fifth-largest Latino state in the country. Chicago's Latino precincts are dense, organized, and politically consequential.
So how much of that $50 million went toward Spanish-language outreach? According to our research: **nearly zero.** We're talking about amounts so small they don't register as a rounding error on a $35 million campaign budget.
Compare that to Texas, where the primary results told a completely different story. James Talarico's campaign and its supporting super PACs invested deliberately in Latino outreach and the results in the Rio Grande Valley and other Latino-heavy districts were dramatic. That's not a coincidence. That's cause and effect.
The Illinois outcome isn't just a missed opportunity. It's a data point in a pattern we've been documenting for years: campaigns of both parties continue to treat Latino voters as an afterthought, assume passive loyalty, and then express bewilderment when the numbers don't move the way they expected.
Here's what we know: you cannot win Latino voters you are not talking to. This isn't theory. This is thirty-plus years of combined field experience telling you exactly what the data shows.
And before Republicans feel smug about any of this: we see you too.
* * *
### The "Hiccup" That Wasn't
This week, [Punchbowl News reported that House Republicans have begun conducting focus groups and internal polling after growing alarm about their standing with Latino voters.](https://substack.com/redirect/683631fd-d466-4fc3-94df-ab54fcddf37e?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) Speaker Mike Johnson reportedly described the problem as a "hiccup."
This is not a hiccup. This is the fastest collapse of a political honeymoon in modern American history. After the 2024 election, when Donald Trump made genuine, historic inroads with Latino voters, breaking roughly 50/50 in some key demographics, Republicans had an opening unlike anything the party had seen in a generation with this constituency.
They torched it in under 60 days. Whoops.
ICE operations targeting families with deep community roots. Tariff policies hammering Latino small business owners and construction workers. A governing posture that treats the same voters it courted as threats to be managed rather than constituents to be served.
Mike's book, [The Latino Century](https://substack.com/redirect/36a45bd9-91dd-4c42-910b-8d8fc6319b63?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), opens with a simple thesis: all Republicans have to do to win Latino voters is stop being racist. The events of the past 90 days suggest that is, in fact, harder than it sounds.
The focus groups are a good sign. The framing as a "hiccup" is not. If you walked into the room thinking this is a messaging problem, you walked in with the wrong diagnosis.

### The Latino Vote Summit: It's Real, June 23rd, Mark Your Calendar
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/b2c654de-f1ef-44af-9f00-45a595c19027?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
We've been teasing this for a while. It's time to make it official.
**The Latino Vote Summit is happening on June 23rd in Washington, D.C.**
This is an invite-only, one-day convening of Latino leaders from across the ideological and professional spectrum: labor, business, environmental, civic, political. The explicit goal is to get the 60-70% of issues our community agrees on into the same room and start building toward a coherent, unified Latino political agenda.
No bomb-throwing. No red-versus-blue foxhole politics. No outside speakers. **Latino voices only.**
The centerpiece of the day will be a Latino town hall at lunch featuring a sitting U.S. senator who will take unscripted questions directly from attendees about what the Latino community demands from its elected officials. There will be press in the room. That's intentional.
Chuck and Mike have been talking about doing something like this for years. The podcast has built the audience and the credibility to make it mean something. The political moment makes it necessary.
If you want to be considered for an invitation, send us a DM or drop your info in the comments. Space is extremely limited and this will fill fast.

And the announcement we've been building toward for years. | | ---|---|--- | | | Forwarded this email? ? for more ? A bombshell investigation. A $50 million blind spot. A Republican "hiccup." And the announcement we've been building toward for years. | | , , and | Mar 25 | | | | | ---|---|---|---|--- | | | | | | | | | | | | | ---|---|--- | | ---|---|--- | | ---|---|--- The Chavez Reckoning , co-founder of the United Farm Workers, labor movement icon, and for millions of Mexican Americans, a figure of near-mythical stature. Thanks for reading! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work. The allegations are serious. And the response from the UFW () only adds weight to what is already an overwhelming evidentiary record. We won't pretend this is easy to process. For Chuck, who has spent his career as one of the country's few prominent Latino labor leaders, this is personal. For Mike, who grew up in the shadow of the UFW organizing drives in Ventura County, it cuts deep in a different way. But personal discomfort is not an excuse to look away. What we're watching in real time is what happens when a community built its political identity around a single human being rather than a set of values and a movement. The statues, the schools, the holiday, the bust in the Oval Office. All of it now carries an asterisk. And the question before us isn't whether that asterisk exists. It's what we do next. Here's our argument: the movement was always bigger than the man. , represents what this fight was actually about. The farm workers who organized, who went on strike, who built collective power from nothing represent what this fight was actually about. That work doesn't disappear because its most famous face has been exposed as deeply, profoundly flawed. But this moment also demands something of us politically. We have to stop deifying people. Full stop. The cult of personality is dangerous in every direction. Whether the idol is Cesar Chavez or Donald Trump. When we place human beings on marble pedestals, we make ourselves vulnerable to exactly this kind of collapse. The antidote isn't cynicism. It's investing in ideas, institutions, and movements. Not individual saviors. Illinois: $50 Million and Not One Dollar for Us On the same day the Chavez story broke, , and the results handed us a perfect case study in exactly what's wrong with how both parties approach the Latino vote. The race featured three well-funded candidates: Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi, Lt. Governor Juliana Stratton, and Congresswoman Robin Kelly. Combined hard money and outside spending topped $50 million. Governor Pritzker alone dropped $5 million into a super PAC backing Stratton. Illinois has 1.1 million registered Latino voters. It is the fifth-largest Latino state in the country. Chicago's Latino precincts are dense, organized, and politically consequential. So how much of that $50 million went toward Spanish-language outreach? According to our research: nearly zero. We're talking about amounts so small they don't register as a rounding error on a $35 million campaign budget. Compare that to Texas, where the primary results told a completely different story. James Talarico's campaign and its supporting super PACs invested deliberately in Latino outreach and the results in the Rio Grande Valley and other Latino-heavy districts were dramatic. That's not a coincidence. That's cause and effect. The Illinois outcome isn't just a missed opportunity. It's a data point in a pattern we've been documenting for years: campaigns of both parties continue to treat Latino voters as an afterthought, assume passive loyalty, and then express bewilderment when the numbers don't move the way they expected. Here's what we know: you cannot win Latino voters you are not talking to. This isn't theory. This is thirty-plus years of combined field experience telling you exactly what the data shows. And before Republicans feel smug about any of this: we see you too. The "Hiccup" That Wasn't This week, Speaker Mike Johnson reportedly described the problem as a "hiccup." This is not a hiccup. This is the fastest collapse of a political honeymoon in modern American history. After the 2024 election, when Donald Trump made genuine, historic inroads with Latino voters, breaking roughly 50/50 in some key demographics, Republicans had an opening unlike anything the party had seen in a generation with this constituency. They torched it in under 60 days. Whoops. ICE operations targeting families with deep community roots. Tariff policies hammering Latino small business owners and construction workers. A governing posture that treats the same voters it courted as threats to be managed rather than constituents to be served. Mike's book, , opens with a simple thesis: all Republicans have to do to win Latino voters is stop being racist. The events of the past 90 days suggest that is, in fact, harder than it sounds. The focus groups are a good sign. The framing as a "hiccup" is not. If you walked into the room thinking this is a messaging problem, you walked in with the wrong diagnosis. The Latino Vote Summit: It's Real, June 23rd, Mark Your Calendar | | ---|---|--- We've been teasing this for a while. It's time to make it official. The Latino Vote Summit is happening on June 23rd in Washington, D.C. This is an invite-only, one-day convening of Latino leaders from across the ideological and professional spectrum: labor, business, environmental, civic, political. The explicit goal is to get the 60-70% of issues our community agrees on into the same room and start building toward a coherent, unified Latino political agenda. No bomb-throwing. No red-versus-blue foxhole politics. No outside speakers. Latino voices only. The centerpiece of the day will be a Latino town hall at lunch featuring a sitting U.S. senator who will take unscripted questions directly from attendees about what the Latino community demands from its elected officials. There will be press in the room. That's intentional. Chuck and Mike have been talking about doing something like this for years. The podcast has built the audience and the credibility to make it mean something. The political moment makes it necessary. If you want to be considered for an invitation, send us a DM or drop your info in the comments. Space is extremely limited and this will fill fast. Peter,
The last year of the Trump presidency has been nothing short of a full blown assault.
MAGA has thrown out the rule book and is beating the living hell out of us.
The nation is turning on them but they don't care, they aren't worried about public opinion. Rather than face the music at the polls in November they will circumvent the voters, redistrict, and enshrine one party rule.
We could stop them but so far we haven't.
There are more congressional seats in blue states than there are in red states. If Republicans redistricted every state they control (which they are in the process of doing) and we redistricted every one of our states - their plan would backfire.
But Trump is betting that we won't have the guts to fight back and punch him in the nose.
California and Virginia showed him otherwise with their redistricts. Now Colorado is joining them with the announcement of Colorado Draws the Line's redistricting ballot measure that will give Democrats up to 3 additional seats in Congress. We're ready to throw a knockout punch.

The Duck River in Tennessee is widely recognized as one of the most biodiverse rivers in North America and the world. It hosts over 150 fish species and 60+ freshwater mussel species, exceeding the fish diversity of all European rivers combined. It is a critical, yet endangered, hotspot for aquatic life, featuring numerous unique species.
Dustin J. Kittle is an attorney who represents clients in the Birmingham, Alabama area. Dustin Kittle is recognized by peers and was selected to Rising Stars based off of 12 indicators including peer recognition and professional achievement in legal practice.
Dustin Kittle chose to pursue a career in law after completing undergraduate studies. He attended Samford University Cumberland School of Law and graduated in 2006.
Being selected to Rising Stars is limited to a small number of attorneys in each state. As one of the few attorneys to garner the distinction of Rising Stars, Dustin Kittle has earned the respect of peers as one of the top-rated attorneys in the nation.
In this episode, Dustin Kittle and I delve into crucial issues facing small farms and food production quality, preserving Duck river, eminent domain and much more...

clean_body: | | | Friend - Here’s my plan for how we win this election: This is a ground game. This is person-to-person, human-to-human, mukluk telegraph. For those in the Lower 48, mukluk telegraph is a saying we have in the Bush that basically amounts to gossip. It’s passing along a message through our conversations with one another, which is the only way information can really spread in some parts of the Last Frontier! In a state as vast and rural as ours, there really is no other way to reach every Alaskan. That’s why it’s so important for us to travel to their communities and have those person-to-person conversations. There are 585,000 square miles in this state — bigger than Texas, California, and Montana combined. And we’re going to criss-cross it in its entirety. But to be honest with you, reaching every community will be expensive. More than 80% of our communities can only be reached by plane, boat or snow machine. And when we are able to drive, gas up here costs much more than it does in most of the Lower 48! But we don’t have another option. I’m running for U.S. Senate to fight for all Alaskans, and I’m committed to bringing every borough into this fight with me. That’s why I’m asking for your support today. We need to take our message across Alaska, and we can’t do it without your help. ** you've saved your payment information with ActBlue Express, your split donation to Mary Peltola and Able Dems will go through immediately. | | Dear Fellow Conservative,You know it and I know it -- Congress is broken. Politicians have turned “serving the people” into “serving themselves.” They use their positions to get richer and richer every year, while you and I get left behind.Left-wing radicals like Ilhan Omar, Rashida Tlaib, and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez work to destroy our country from within. And Washington never fixes anything. **[Today, WE THE PEOPLE have a chance to do something about it when you sign your “Time for Term Limits” petition and submit it in the next 72 hours.](https://email.updates.conservativeinnovation.com/c/eJyUkM2OmzAUhZ_G7ED-N1l4wQxhFKlU1WhEl5axTWIJ2wgM8_oVafoA3d177o_O-X73qtd-9vH-UwcnzeHVuqlvF52zOa1OmwcKfp59iovOq8IQ8xKSErNzDxVWGssJLpxEQlDKLhCy4iFrhtjIkOCihpMweBICTuOlroUZKZx44eX5CRLMkECckqrmIxaIXxh3GhIGAYX7YnV2W2VS3Nx66OwP52NMZ5ViZVIoZvnIedkAaQDuAO500Eab53h1x1GZBHC3aMytnRgVBjEz2ZqyGpBuz0FtaV-NA6R9az_Kz-sAMD_l4KzfAyDttX8pRodF-3sEpP1rHHH11n6opm--1I_-9vXsPq-D-tWU78PtdZYNIO37cMPlv7jFKu3yfRLduAAU3oP28zNL_n_6h8R_AgAA__9tzI1E)** Our Founding Fathers never intended for government service to be a permanent career. George Washington famously served just two terms — then went home.Our Founding Fathers also said our government was made for a “moral and religious people.” And they understood that if that moral compass broke down, Congress could easily steer America in the wrong direction, become a do-nothing body, or make government a gravy train for themselves.That’s why they included a powerful safeguard in our Constitution -- an escape hatch -- enshrined in Article V. If Congress ever became too corrupt to fix itself, Article V. says the states can use this provision in the Constitution to act.34 state legislatures can call a convention, propose term limits -- and Congress can’t do a thing about it. [**Here at AMAC Action, we have led the term limits movement in the past, and we are ready to put our efforts behind the movement once again.**](https://email.updates.conservativeinnovation.com/c/eJyUkM2OmzAUhZ_G7ED-N1l4wQxhFKlU1WhEl5axTWIJ2wgM8_oVafoA3d177o_O-X73qtd-9vH-UwcnzeHVuqlvF52zOa1OmwcKfp59iovOq8IQ8xKSErNzDxVWGssJLpxEQlDKLhCy4iFrhtjIkOCihpMweBICTuOlroUZKZx44eX5CRLMkECckqrmIxaIXxh3GhIGAYX7YnV2W2VS3Nx66OwP52NMZ5ViZVIoZvnIedkAaQDuAO500Eab53h1x1GZBHC3aMytnRgVBjEz2ZqyGpBuz0FtaV-NA6R9az_Kz-sAMD_l4KzfAyDttX8pRodF-3sEpP1rHHH11n6opm--1I_-9vXsPq-D-tWU78PtdZYNIO37cMPlv7jFKu3yfRLduAAU3oP28zNL_n_6h8R_AgAA__9tzI1E)

#
Just look at what Republicans have been doing in Congress.
They have been voting to advance cuts on hundreds of billions of dollars from Medicaid, veterans' benefits, and Social Security **so that they can give it to the billionaires who elected them** , in the form of tax cuts and sweetheart government contracts to companies like SpaceX.
They know that it is deeply unpopular. They know that it hurts you.
But they are not here to serve us. They are here to serve themselves and the billionaires who have paid them. **Oligarchy**.
They know that the only chance they have to get away with such an unpopular agenda — to get away with stealing in plain view — is to stoke deep divisions among us along lines of race, identity, and culture to keep us distracted.
This has been the Big Money Playbook — not just now, but for generations.
And that is why **Donald Trump is not an aberration**.
He is the logical and inevitable conclusion to an American political system that has been dominated by corporate and dark money.
And if we are here to defeat him, **we must defeat the system that created him**.
**That means that we choose to out-organize the oligarchy**. We will, and we must, do away with the power of big money in our politics.

| | Hello folks — Last month, I watched Jeff Crank’s virtual town hall (virtual, because he apparently doesn’t want to face voters in person). During that event, he said something that stopped me cold: _“I’m not here to support the VA system.”_ **As a decorated Veteran who served two combat tours in Afghanistan, I can tell you why that statement is unacceptable.** Veterans and military families rely on the VA every single day for healthcare, employment services, and housing assistance. And right now, that system is already under enormous strain. The VA has cut more than 14,000 medical positions, and the _New York Times_ reports doctor shortages in nearly 90% of departments, leaving Veterans waiting longer for care. **And while this crisis grows, Jeff Crank has been completely silent.**

clean_body: | | | | | Hello folks — Last month, I watched Jeff Crank’s virtual town hall (virtual, because he apparently doesn’t want to face voters in person). During that event, he said something that stopped me cold: “I’m not here to support the VA system.” As a decorated Veteran who served two combat tours in Afghanistan, I can tell you why that statement is unacceptable. Veterans and military families rely on the VA every single day for healthcare, employment services, and housing assistance. And right now, that system is already under enormous strain. The VA has cut more than 14,000 medical positions, and the New York Times reports doctor shortages in nearly 90% of departments, leaving Veterans waiting longer for care. Picture the scene in the Situation Room, not 1962 but 2026: aides hunched over screens, not tracking missiles but monitoring GPU shipments and data-center permits. The technology that once promised to augment human decision-making **[now races ahead of the deciders themselves.](https://substack.com/redirect/46c7e648-96ad-42ee-ac74-bf0031c3b287?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)**[ ](https://substack.com/redirect/46c7e648-96ad-42ee-ac74-bf0031c3b287?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/37363a45-15f3-41ff-834c-780f898a06da?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
On March 20, the White House released its **[National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence](https://substack.com/redirect/7c4129ab-f2da-494c-8227-89b8235a3868?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** --a document that, for all its polished objectives, reads like an elegant white flag on behalf of bureaucracy. The federal government, long accustomed to writing the rules of the game, has quietly acknowledged that the game has changed.
The framework's core thesis arrives early and without apology: America needs "one federal AI policy, not a 50-state patchwork." Director Michael Kratsios put it plainly on X the same day: "This gets us there."

What remains unsaid--but hangs in every paragraph--is the reason such preemption is suddenly urgent.

# **[JPMorgan Calls It a'Core Holding.' Most Retirement Accounts Hold Zero](https://substack.com/redirect/bdcdc5a0-513d-41ab-8de3-70f11f005385?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)**
If you're 55 or older and your IRA has no gold -- JPMorgan just made that expensive.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/bdcdc5a0-513d-41ab-8de3-70f11f005385?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
They've raised their 2026 gold forecast to $6,300. Laid out a credible path to $8,000. And officially called gold a "core holding" -- not a crisis hedge, not a speculation. A core holding.
Here's why that matters if you're near retirement:
Most Americans hold less than 1% in gold. When that shifts -- even slightly -- demand collides with limited supply. Prices don't drift. They reprice. Fast.
Gold already broke $5,000. Already outperformed the S&P 500 in 2026.
If you're living off your savings -- or will be soon -- you don't get to wait for the second leg up before deciding.

* * *
* * *
AI no longer develops in tidy DARPA labs or corporate sandboxes; it proliferates through consumer apps, enterprise tools, and adversarial smuggling rings running out of the most unexpected of places. Just this week the co-founder of American firm Super Micro Computer was **[busted for smuggling export restricted chips to China.](https://substack.com/redirect/82b98350-8f99-4a02-9bc9-2c27a43ee7be?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)**
The technology is already here--embedded in classrooms, boardrooms, campaign war rooms, and Senate staff terminals (**[which recently greenlit ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot](https://substack.com/redirect/e8dc2573-a0df-4b15-98f7-04be2bc1d59c?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)**). The issue of grappling with the new "AI world" is already here. Lawmakers are no longer setting the pace; they are chasing it.
Consider the child-safety provisions. The framework calls on Congress to mandate _**" age-assurance requirements"**_ for platforms likely accessed by minors and to curb risks of sexual exploitation and self-harm. Sensible, even necessary. Yet the language betrays a shift in power dynamics: government is reduced to requesting tools that parents and platforms must implement because the tech itself scales risk beyond adult supervision.
Similarly, on energy infrastructure, the document urges protection for residential ratepayers from electricity-price spikes tied to AI data centers. Again, prudent--but note the framing. The administration is not commanding new power plants or capping compute; it is pleading that builders not punish ordinary households while they scale the very systems that drive economic growth.

* * *

[ Support What We Do](https://substack.com/redirect/37363a45-15f3-41ff-834c-780f898a06da?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
* * *
* * *
The most revealing passages concern copyright and speech. On training data, the White House states it _**" believes that training of AI models on copyrighted material does not violate copyright laws"**_ yet defers resolution to the courts. That is not leadership; it is delegation. On speech, the framework insists Congress prevent government from _**" coercing technology providers, including AI providers, to ban, compel, or alter content based on partisan or ideological agendas."**_ A welcome bulwark against censorship--but observe the asymmetry. The state, once the presumed arbiter of truth, now asks to be restrained from meddling in the platforms it increasingly relies upon.
Critics--particularly those nostalgic for heavier-handed approaches--will argue this light-touch stance abdicates responsibility. They point to real dangers: deepfakes in elections, algorithmic bias, concentrated compute power. Fair enough. Yet the counterpoint is sharper: Every attempt at comprehensive top-down control with emerging tech has either slowed American progress or pushed development offshore. The framework's six objectives--child protection, energy equity, free speech, liability reform, innovation acceleration, and national-security hardening--strike a balance that favors builders over bureaucrats. Preempting state regimes is not anti-federalism; it is anti-fragmentation in a domain where speed has been proven to determine dominance.
The document's true significance lies in what it does not do:
* **There is no call for a new federal AI agency,**
* **There is no sweeping moratorium,**
* **There is no mandatory safety certifications.**

All things that could choke open-source efforts and inhibit the prevalence and growth of American AI dominance.
Instead, it leans into the private sector's comparative advantage: rapid iteration, massive capital deployment, global talent attraction. The Trump administration understands what previous administrations did not--that trying to fully control AI is like trying to bottle lightning. The smart play is to channel it, not contain it.
Of course, risks remain. A single national standard _**could**_ entrench incumbents if poorly drafted. Energy demands _**could**_ still strain grids without parallel infrastructure reform, but adversaries--China chief among them--**will** exploit any hesitation or faltering missteps in this area and we already have evidence of what that exploitation looks like in practice.
America pioneered the idea of offensive capability drones with the Predator in the War on Terror but two decades later the skies of Ukraine and the Persian Gulf are swarmed by cheap light weight hunter killer drones that are not American and their existence has had global ramifications. The same mistake cannot be made with AI. The stakes are too high.
The latest framework's realism is its strength: it treats AI as an economic and strategic asset already in motion, not a hypothetical menace to be tamed at some point in the future. This is what NOT "kicking the can down the road" looks like in practice.
In the end, this is less a policy triumph than an intellectual pivot. Washington has stopped pretending it can out-engineer the engineers a final acceptance of what the Crypto industry has been arguing for years. That the real winners will be those who build fastest and smartest under a stable, minimal federal guardrail. That's the play. Builders, your court.

Lawmakers are no longer setting the pace; they are desperately chasing it | | | Mar 25| | | ∙| | Guest post ---|---|--- | | | | | | | | | | | | Picture the scene in the Situation Room, not 1962 but 2026: aides hunched over screens, not tracking missiles but monitoring GPU shipments and data-center permits. The technology that once promised to augment human decision-making | | ---|---|--- On March 20, the White House released its --a document that, for all its polished objectives, reads like an elegant white flag on behalf of bureaucracy. The federal government, long accustomed to writing the rules of the game, has quietly acknowledged that the game has changed. The framework's core thesis arrives early and without apology: America needs "one federal AI policy, not a 50-state patchwork." Director Michael Kratsios put it plainly on X the same day: "This gets us there." What remains unsaid--but hangs in every paragraph--is the reason such preemption is suddenly urgent. Sponsored by If you're 55 or older and your IRA has no gold -- JPMorgan just made that expensive. | | ---|---|--- They've raised their 2026 gold forecast to $6,300. Laid out a credible path to $8,000. And officially called gold a "core holding" -- not a crisis hedge, not a speculation. A core holding. Here's why that matters if you're near retirement: Most Americans hold less than 1% in gold. When that shifts -- even slightly -- demand collides with limited supply. Prices don't drift. They reprice. Fast. Gold already broke $5,000. Already outperformed the S&P 500 in 2026. If you're living off your savings -- or will be soon -- you don't get to wait for the second leg up before deciding. The free 2026 Info Guide shows you: Why JPMorgan is calling gold a "core holding" for retirement portfolios What the $6,300 -> $8,000 path means for people near retirement How to add physical gold to your existing IRA or 401(k) -- no penalties, no tax hit, done in days AI no longer develops in tidy DARPA labs or corporate sandboxes; it proliferates through consumer apps, enterprise tools, and adversarial smuggling rings running out of the most unexpected of places. Just this week the co-founder of American firm Super Micro Computer was The technology is already here--embedded in classrooms, boardrooms, campaign war rooms, and Senate staff terminals (). The issue of grappling with the new "AI world" is already here. Lawmakers are no longer setting the pace; they are chasing it. Consider the child-safety provisions. The framework calls on Congress to mandate " age-assurance requirements" for platforms likely accessed by minors and to curb risks of sexual exploitation and self-harm. Sensible, even necessary. Yet the language betrays a shift in power dynamics: government is reduced to requesting tools that parents and platforms must implement because the tech itself scales risk beyond adult supervision. Similarly, on energy infrastructure, the document urges protection for residential ratepayers from electricity-price spikes tied to AI data centers. Again, prudent--but note the framing. The administration is not commanding new power plants or capping compute; it is pleading that builders not punish ordinary households while they scale the very systems that drive economic growth. The most revealing passages concern copyright and speech. On training data, the White House states it " believes that training of AI models on copyrighted material does not violate copyright laws" yet defers resolution to the courts. That is not leadership; it is delegation. On speech, the framework insists Congress prevent government from " coercing technology providers, including AI providers, to ban, compel, or alter content based on partisan or ideological agendas." A welcome bulwark against censorship--but observe the asymmetry. The state, once the presumed arbiter of truth, now asks to be restrained from meddling in the platforms it increasingly relies upon. Critics--particularly those nostalgic for heavier-handed approaches--will argue this light-touch stance abdicates responsibility. They point to real dangers: deepfakes in elections, algorithmic bias, concentrated compute power. Fair enough. Yet the counterpoint is sharper: Every attempt at comprehensive top-down control with emerging tech has either slowed American progress or pushed development offshore. The framework's six objectives--child protection, energy equity, free speech, liability reform, innovation acceleration, and national-security hardening--strike a balance that favors builders over bureaucrats. Preempting state regimes is not anti-federalism; it is anti-fragmentation in a domain where speed has been proven to determine dominance. The document's true significance lies in what it does not do: There is no call for a new federal AI agency, There is no sweeping moratorium, There is no mandatory safety certifications. All things that could choke open-source efforts and inhibit the prevalence and growth of American AI dominance. Instead, it leans into the private sector's comparative advantage: rapid iteration, massive capital deployment, global talent attraction. The Trump administration understands what previous administrations did not--that trying to fully control AI is like trying to bottle lightning. The smart play is to channel it, not contain it. Of course, risks remain. A single national standard could entrench incumbents if poorly drafted. Energy demands could still strain grids without parallel infrastructure reform, but adversaries--China chief among them--will exploit any hesitation or faltering missteps in this area and we already have evidence of what that exploitation looks like in practice. America pioneered the idea of offensive capability drones with the Predator in the War on Terror but two decades later the skies of Ukraine and the Persian Gulf are swarmed by cheap light weight hunter killer drones that are not American and their existence has had global ramifications. The same mistake cannot be made with AI. The stakes are too high. The latest framework's realism is its strength: it treats AI as an economic and strategic asset already in motion, not a hypothetical menace to be tamed at some point in the future. This is what NOT "kicking the can down the road" looks like in practice. In the end, this is less a policy triumph than an intellectual pivot. Washington has stopped pretending it can out-engineer the engineers a final acceptance of what the Crypto industry has been arguing for years. That the real winners will be those who build fastest and smartest under a stable, minimal federal guardrail. That's the play. Builders, your court. | | Lifе and death Son of Mykhailo Sulyma, Ivan came from a petty noble (szlachta) family. He was born in Rohoshchi (next to Chernihiv). He served as an estate overseer for Stanisław Żółkiewski and later the family of Daniłowicze who inherited his lands; for that service in 1620 he was awarded three villages: Sulimówka, Kuczakiw and Lebedyn. Аll the villages todаy belong to the Boryspil Raion, Kyiv Oblast. His sons included Stepan (died 1659), a captain of Boryspil company, and Fedir (died 1691), a colonel of Pereiaslav regiment. He became popular among the unregistered Cossacks, leading them on campaigns to plunder Crimea and other Ottoman vassal territories. For organizing a revolt on an Ottoman slave galley and freeing Christian slaves[1] he received a medal from Pope Paul V himself. Eventually, Sulyma reached the rank of the hetman, which he held from 1628 to 1629 and 1630 to 1635. In 1635, after returning from an expedition to Black Sea against the Ottomans, he decided to rebel against the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, which at that time controlled most of the Cossack territories, and whose nobility was trying to turn militant Cossacks into serfs.[citation needed] Ivan Sulyma took part in numerous campaigns of Sagaidachny against Tatars and Turks. In particular, it was the famous capture of Kafa (modern Theodosia), the main center of the slave trade on the Black Sea, Trapezont, Izmail, and also two attacks on Tsaregrad. On the night of 3 to 4 August 1635 he took the newly constructed Kodak fortress by surprise, burning it and executing its crew of about 200 people under Jean Marion. Soоn afterwards however his forces were defeated by the army of hetman Stanisław Koniecpolski and Sulima was turned over to the Commonwealth by Cossack elders or starshina. Together with several other leaders of his rebellion, Hetman Sulyma was executed in Warsaw on 12 December 1635. At first, the Polish King Władysław IV Waza, known for his friendly attitude towards the Cossacks, was hesitant to execute Sulyma, especially since he was a person upon whom the Pope himself bestowed his medal. However, pressured by the nobility who wanted to show that no rebellions against the 'established оrder' would be tolerated, the оrder for an execution was given; after being tortured, Sulyma was cut to pieces and his body parts were hung on the city walls of Warsaw

And right now, one startup appears to be running the same play — with a piece of hardware that's even more common than doorbells or thermostats. The light switch. The average home has 20 to 30 light switches. Most haven't been updated since the house was built. They're simple, mechanical, and completely disconnected from the rest of the home. iotty is replacing them with Wi-Fi-connected smart switches made from tempered glass with touch controls and customizable backlighting. But the real value isn't the switch itself — it's what happens after installation. Each switch becomes an intelligent node in the home. It can automate lighting based on who's in the room. Monitor energy usage in real time. Connect to Alexa, Google, and Apple HomeKit. And serve as the foundation for a fully automated living space. Ring proved that a connected doorbell could become a security platform. Nest proved that a connected thermostat could become an energy platform. iotty is proving that a connected light switch can become a home automation platform. And the traction is already there: 100,000+ devices installed worldwide $13M+ in cumulative revenue 70%+ gross margins 4.9-star rating across 1,500+ reviews $408 average order value with $630+ 12-month customer lifetime value That last number matters. Customers keep buying more switches after the first install. Room by room, iotty becomes embedded in the entire home — just like Ring cameras started at the front door and spread to backyards, garages, and hallways. The smart home market is expected to reach $537 billion by 2030. Major players like Amazon, Apple, Google, and Samsung are all investing heavily in this space. Ring and Nest got acquired because they built the hardware layer that those ecosystems needed. iotty is building the next piece of that same layer. Right now, shares are available to everyday investors at just $1.00 each. However, April 15 is the last chance to invest and earn up to 30% bonus shares before the round closes and this share price is gone. As with any early-stage investment, there are risks involved. But for those who see the pattern — the same one that made early Ring and Nest investors very happy — this could be a compelling opportunity to get in early. Addressing Affordability, Lowering Costs, and Protecting the Regional Economy** What people in Northwest Washington are facing:
* Higher prices tied to tariffs and economic instability
* Dependence on major regional employers (especially aerospace)
* Supply chain and trade disruptions that affect workers and businesses

What I am doing:
* Supporting efforts to end tariffs that raise costs for consumers and businesses, and increasing prices on groceries, energy, and health care.
* Advocating for job growth in aerospace, including the upcoming Boeing production expansion that creates jobs for regional workers.
* Passing federal funding packages that invest in jobs, education, and infrastructure.

**2\. Infrastructure, Transportation, and Local Project Funding** What people in Northwest Washington are facing:
* Aging transportation infrastructure
* Need for transit and port investments
* Regional economic growth tied to mobility and logistics

What I am doing:
* Securing federal infrastructure funding for projects across Northwest Washington.
* Opening applications for Community Project Funding that directs federal dollars to local governments and nonprofits.
* Bringing money home to WA-02 to support investments that strengthen infrastructure, community facilities, and economic development.

**3\. Disaster Recovery and Climate Resilience** What people in Northwest Washington are facing:
* Recent flooding has made disaster recovery and climate resilience an immediate concern.
* Damaged infrastructure, homes, and businesses.
* Increasing frequency and severity of climate-related disasters.

What I am doing:
* Supporting federal disaster assistance and pushing for a major disaster declaration to repair damaged infrastructure.
* Connecting communities with resources like the new SBA loans to help businesses rebuild after floods.
* Raising the alarm about the real-world impacts of climate change on Northwest Washington communities.

**4\. Public Safety and the Opioid Crisis** What people in Northwest Washington are facing:
* The opioid epidemic continues to affect communities across Northwest Washington
* Need for treatment, prevention, and law enforcement resources

What I am doing:
* Securing federal funding for addiction recovery programs, public safety initiatives, and law enforcement efforts to disrupt trafficking.
* Framing the opioid crisis as a community-wide challenge requiring federal support and coordination.

**5\. Accountability, Democracy, Oversight, and Supporting Our Servicepeople** What people in Northwest Washington are facing:
* Impacts of dark money in elections
* A reckless approach to immigration enforcement
* An undermining of Congressional authority on war powers

What I am doing:
* Reintroducing the DISCLOSE Act to end dark money in elections and increase transparency in political spending.
* Opposing DHS funding proposals that lack accountability for ICE enforcement actions.
* Voting to require congressional authorization for military hostilities involving Iran.
* Supporting Coast Guard investments and maritime safety infrastructure.
* Launching community initiatives recognizing veterans and servicemembers.

**All of this work reflects what I believe government should do: deliver practical results and make life better for the people it serves.** But continuing that work will require building a strong campaign this election year. Republicans are already preparing to defend their House majority, and taking back the House will be critical to restoring stability in Washington and making progress on the issues that matter most to Northwest Washington. subject: Three Votes. One Week. Your Values on the Line.
disclaimer_text: Paid for by Vote Baumgartner for Congress • PO Box 8508, Spokane, WA 99203 [Website](https://hotmail
body:
Last week I voted to protect hunters, balance the budget, and deport fraudsters. Democrats opposed all three. End-of-quarter deadline: March 31.
| [ ](https://hotmail.us21.list-manage.com/track/click?u=91b93e6889137ccb3f3fef037&id=6f5e10db38&e=5a45b9550e)
---
| This Week in Congress THREE VOTES.
THREE FIGHTS.
YOUR VALUES ON THE LINE. Democrats opposed every single one.
---
Friend, Last week, three votes came to the House floor that tell you everything you need to know about the difference between conservatives and the Democrat Party. I was proud to vote YES on all three. Democrats opposed every one.
| | Vote #1 Protecting Hunters & Anglers | ✔
---|---
H.R. 556 -- PASSED 215-202 ● I voted YES
Conservatives have always believed in protecting the right to hunt and fish. The Biden administration tried to ban lead ammunition on over 3 million acres of federal land -- not because the science demanded it, but to settle lawsuits with activist groups. That would have driven up costs and closed off access for sportsmen across the country. In Eastern Washington, hunting and fishing are a way of life. I voted to keep bureaucrats in D.C. from taking that away. The NRA, Congressional Sportsmen's Foundation, and American Sportfishing Association all backed this bill. **202 members voted no.**
| | Vote #2 Balanced Budget Amendment | ✔
---|---
H.J.Res. 139 -- 211-207 (needed 2⁄3 supermajority) ● I voted YES

So if you want to help continue making progress for kids—such as the historic highs in student achievement and the biggest expansion of preschool in state history—I could really use your help today. If you can, please:

* **Forward this to a friend** — truly one of the most impactful things you can do; if you forward this to three friends, we can expand our reach dramatically.

Three quick things that make a real difference.
Thanks so much for being in this with me. More updates soon.

Voter Action Project [https://voteractionproject.org/]
AP: Trump casts Florida mail ballot as he pushes Congress to severely limit that voting option [http://secure.actblue.com/donate/ifvap-democracy?refcode=032526_2&amount=25]
Team: Donald Trump voted by mail. No, we're not referring to his well-documented past usage of the practice.
No, after years of attacking vote-by-mail, countless late-night Truth Social rants, and several executive orders within the last year trying to end, or at least curtail, mail-in voting, Donald Trump voted by mail this week, in a Florida special election held on March 24, 2026 . He could have gone to an early voting site when he was at Mar-A-Lago the week before the election, but he chose to submit a mailed ballot instead, according to Palm Beach County voter records.
To be honest, we here at Voter Action Project are glad he did. We believe every eligible American deserves to vote in the manner that is easiest for them to participate. That's because we believe that the act of participation is the most important part, not what method you use to cast your ballot.
It's worth noting, however, how he's very willing to use this tool to help himself and make his own voice heard, but he wants to restrict it for everyone else if it seems like it might not benefit him. The pattern is completely clear, and his self-interest drives every decision and statement he makes about voting.
So next time you run into that anti-voting family member, friend, or neighbor, just let them know: Trump himself chose to skip voting in person while in Florida and voted by mail in 2026.
Onward,
The Voter Action Project Team

We have no wealthy backers in the shadows, just regular people standing up for the right to vote and offering what they can, a little at a time. name: Deb Haaland
subject: From my kitchen to yours: green chile chicken posole
disclaimer_text: PAID FOR AND AUTHORIZED BY DEB FOR NEW MEXICO**
body:
Cooking has always been a way for me to foster connection and build community.

| | |
---
Hey there – it’s Deb.
One thing you should know about me is that**I love to cook.**
My love of cooking New Mexican cuisine started early, thanks to the hours I spent watching my grandmother bake bread in her mud oven and stir huge pots of posole. She wouldn’t let us kids in the kitchen while she cooked, but I’d perch myself outside and watch her through the window for hours. I still hold those memories close as I prepare my favorite traditional New Mexican dishes.
[](https://act.debhaaland.com/go/6973?t=1&akid=8491%2E400544%2E9p87C9) _New Mexico chiles – the best in the world!_
**There’s something powerful about connecting with others over a home-cooked meal.** When I was in law school at UNM, I’d make chicken green chile stew for student gatherings, and I made that same dish for my Congressional colleagues during the 2019 winter holiday season. I even cooked chile and tortillas for the water protectors when I traveled to Standing Rock during the protests against the Dakota Access Pipeline.
Cooking became more than a hobby after I decided to start my own salsa business. I worked out of a commercial kitchen and bought my red chile pequin from a farm in northern New Mexico. I’d prepare my salsa and deliver jars to mom-and-pop shops across the state, often with my child Somáh riding with me in the back seat.
[](https://act.debhaaland.com/go/6973?t=2&akid=8491%2E400544%2E9p87C9) _Here’s Somáh posing with jars of my homemade salsa. Kids in New Mexico start early... 🌶️_
**For me, cooking has always been a way to foster connection and build community, which is exactly what we’re doing now as we grow our campaign for New Mexico.** I’ve had the chance to sit down with New Mexicans in living rooms and at kitchen tables to hear about their lives, their struggles, and their hopes for the future. Every conversation is another reminder of the incredibly high stakes in this race – and proof that if we organize around our shared values, we win.
[**Will you donate $5 to power our grassroots campaign? If you donate through this link, I’ll even send you my recipe for green chile chicken posole – one of my favorite dishes to make during the holiday season!**](https://act.debhaaland.com/go/6973?t=3&akid=8491%2E400544%2E9p87C9)
_If you've saved payment information with ActBlue Express, your donation will go through immediately:_ | | | [Donate $10](https://act.debhaaland.com/go/6974?t=4&akid=8491%2E400544%2E9p87C9)
---

---

---

Happy cooking,

Deb 🌶️
P.S. Throughout my life, cooking has helped me bring my community together – and bringing people together is exactly how we’ll win this campaign. [**If you make a donation of any amount through this link, I’ll be sure to send you my recipe for green chile chicken posole so you can cook it for your friends and family.**](https://act.debhaaland.com/go/6973?t=8&akid=8491%2E400544%2E9p87C9)

of anyone in it.

This poll shows that the bet is working.

Since last summer, our team has attended over 300 events across Michigan —
and in that same time, our polling has jumped 8 points.

So now, the question is: How many more people can we reach before our
primary election in August?

[ stdin# ]Jocelyn Benson for Governor
It’s
Jocelyn.

I know you’re hearing from a ton of campaigns right now asking for money.
And I know it seems like the requests are never-ending, so I wanted to
reach out and let you know exactly what your donation goes towards and why
your donation is so important.

[ https://act.jocelynbenson.com/go/3608?t=1001&akid=1569%2E181023%2EmJe3__ ]If you’re short on time, you can click here to make a donation ahead of
our end-of-quarter fundraising deadline:

If you’ve ever wondered exactly what your donation goes towards – I don’t
blame you. Let me give you a little insight.

Your donation goes towards building campaign infrastructure, including
hiring more staff, training volunteers, and ensuring that we can open
campaign offices across Michigan.

Your donation helps us reach more voters, whether that be through our
field program, events, yard signs, or mailers.

Your donation helps us get our ads on air. We’re already up against a $5
million cash infusion from the DeVos family, and we know billionaires and
outside groups will dump even more money in as this race heats up.

All of these things are important to a successful campaign and will help
us win BIG in one of the most competitive battlegrounds in the country.

[ https://act.jocelynbenson.com/go/3608?t=1002&akid=1569%2E181023%2EmJe3__ ]While you might think a donation of $5 or $10 or $50 doesn’t make a
difference, I can assure you it all adds up, especially when my opponents
have the backing of billionaires and special interests. So, will you pitch
in anything to my campaign today to help us keep building the campaign
it’ll take to keep this toss-up seat blue?

If you've saved your payment information with ActBlue Express, your
donation will go through immediately:

Thank you,

Jocelyn

body:
We need your response to this dangerous escalation. | [](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/128049893/610071367/-785282667?nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQMTAvMS84MTM0MiIsDQogICJEaXN0cmlidXRpb25VbmlxdWVJZCI6ICI4M2JlNWM0Yy03YjI4LWYxMTEtOWE0OC0wMDBkM2ExNGI2NDAiLA0KICAiRW1haWxBZGRyZXNzIjogImRwd2lsbGlzNjdAZ21haWwuY29tIg0KfQ%3D%3D&hmac=2HskiqblZhhfibea8FHXGzvN6qVTE2s8qy03Qo-omjM=)
---
Peter, **Right now, the Trump administration is moving even more U.S. troops closer to Iran.** After everything this country has been through, after all the lives lost, after all the pain of endless war, it is unbelievable that we are headed down this road again. Becca has been clear from the start: Congress has the authority to decide whether this country goes to war. Not Donald Trump. Not by impulse. Not without accountability. And not by putting more service members in harm’s way while families here at home are already carrying so much. **That is why we need to hear directly from you today.**
## **Do you support Trump’s decision to send American troops to Iran?**
| **[YES](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/128049894/610071368/1802995197?nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQMTAvMS84MTM0MiIsDQogICJEaXN0cmlidXRpb25VbmlxdWVJZCI6ICI4M2JlNWM0Yy03YjI4LWYxMTEtOWE0OC0wMDBkM2ExNGI2NDAiLA0KICAiRW1haWxBZGRyZXNzIjogImRwd2lsbGlzNjdAZ21haWwuY29tIg0KfQ%3D%3D&hmac=2HskiqblZhhfibea8FHXGzvN6qVTE2s8qy03Qo-omjM=)**

---
Trump is acting like he can do whatever he wants, whenever he wants, with no regard for the Constitution, no regard for Congress, and no regard for the very real human cost.
This isn’t a game. This is about people’s children being sent into danger, military families living with fear, and taxpayer dollars being spent on another war instead of lowering costs, expanding health care, and helping people afford housing and basic needs back home.
**Becca believes we have a responsibility to say this clearly and forcefully: the American people do not want another endless war.**
We hope you’ll take our survey and let us know how you feel.
Thank you for speaking out today,
— Team Becca

subject: UT Austin yesterday: Sun shining, people happy, kittens and butterflies on Speedway.

body:
# [](https://act.betoorourke.com/go/43706?t=1&akid=240766%2E444211%2EtnRmxV)
Namaskaram! Great day at UT Austin yesterday. Sun shining, people happy, kittens and butterflies on Speedway.
Some conversations that stood out... Savanah naturalized in September, got registered to vote with us yesterday. Said it’s a relief to have her citizenship and be able to use it to vote given what’s going on in our country.
I met biotech and public health students who’d just finished coming out of their “Cancerland” class, which they described as the sociology of cancer. They asked “How can we be spending 17% of GDP on health and have a country as sick as ours?”
Ben from El Paso said he wants to finish his education and then come back home and open a PT clinic.
Isabel, a freshman from McAllen said she helped to pass a ballot initiative back home to limit campaign contributions, and told me seeing us doing our work across the state inspired her to get it done.
Sourik told me about being forced to cast a provisional ballot in the last election only to find out it was never counted. So he updated his registration with us to make sure his next vote counts!
I saw the incoming UT student government president, Kiera Dixon (congratulations!).
I met a class of Malayalam students who taught me a few words in Malayalam — Namaskaram is hello — and pointed out that Malayalam is the same forwards and backwards. They also told me that UT is the only place in the country that has a dedicated Malayalam program.
Rama and Reela got registered and told me why.
Our Powered by People volunteers were on fire yesterday — Susan, a registration machine! Thanks to the always awesome University Democrats, to Gabby and Jacob, Adit and Wendy, Lesa, Wes and everyone who came out!
[**If you can afford it, please pitch in $3 to support the incredible work our organizers are doing every single day.**](https://act.betoorourke.com/go/56109?c0=pbp-em-20260325.Wr3rl3&refcode=ema20260325-240766&t=3&akid=240766%2E444211%2EtnRmxV)
Thank you,
Beto

I saw the incoming UT student government president, Kiera Dixon (congratulations!). I met a class of Malayalam students who taught me a few words in Malayalam — Namaskaram is hello — and pointed out that Malayalam is the same forwards and backwards. They also told me that UT is the only place in the country that has a dedicated Malayalam program. Rama and Reela got registered and told me why. Our Powered by People volunteers were on fire yesterday — Susan, a registration machine! Thanks to the always awesome University Democrats, to Gabby and Jacob, Adit and Wendy, Lesa, Wes and everyone who came out! Thank you, Beto

| | Hi friends,

And also, check out our [deep-dive video of the day](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.) on the rise of an unusual candidate in CD4!
Here is a summary of today's top stories:
🏛️ **Under the Golden Dome...** Lawmakers unanimously advanced a bill to [replace César Chávez Day with “Farm Workers Day”](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.) following abuse allegations, while the Cover All Coloradans program has surged from a $14.7 million estimate to over $104 million, adding pressure to the state budget and prompting potential service cuts as [two Democrats tied to the program run for Congress](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.).

🏔️ **Here in Colorado...** A Denver audit found the city’s $178 million homelessness program may have [underreported about $20 million in spending](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.) despite reporting a 45% drop in unsheltered homelessness, while [El Paso County’s clerk withdrew from the state clerks association](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.) citing transparency concerns. Broader debates over accountability are also emerging, with criticism that [some media outlets selectively scrutinize political claims](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.). At the same time, zoning disputes in Lakewood are drawing attention after a homeowner was [blocked from rebuilding a burned single-family home](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.) due to prior rezoning.
🇺🇸**On the National Stage...** The Supreme Court signaled skepticism toward [counting late-arriving mail ballots](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.) ahead of the 2026 midterms, while some Republicans are questioning a [$200 billion Pentagon request](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.) tied to the Iran conflict. Federal regulators also [rejected Colorado oil and gas permits](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.) over weak emissions monitoring, as [Colorado airports continue operating normally](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.) without ICE deployments despite staffing concerns elsewhere.
This is your Mountain Minute for Wednesday, March 25, 2026.

**TODAY'S TOP STORIES**
**[The Democrats who funded Colorado’s 611% Medicaid overrun are running for Congress](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)** BY JEN SCHUMANN, [ROCKY MOUNTAIN VOICE](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)
[](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)
Colorado is staring down a $1 billion budget hole. Disabled kids are losing healthcare. Dental benefits are getting capped at $750 a year. Two Democrats who helped create and fund Cover All Coloradans are now asking voters to send them to Congress.
Shannon Bird stepped away from the statehouse to run full-time. That sets up a primary between Bird and Rep. Manny Rutinel in Colorado’s 8th Congressional District, with Republican incumbent Gabe Evans waiting in November.
It started with HB22-1289 in 2022, opening Medicaid-style coverage to children and pregnant women who otherwise met eligibility but didn’t qualify because of their immigration status. Bird voted yes.
The early estimate was $14.7 million for the fiscal year, tied to an expected enrollment of about 3,700 people—at least that was the projection at the time.

**[El Paso Co. clerk resigns leadership role and pulls county from clerks association over transparency concerns](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)** [ASHE IN AMERICA](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)
* **Largest Colorado county withdraws from clerks association:** El Paso County Clerk Steve Schleiker resigned as vice president of the Colorado County Clerks Association and pulled the state’s largest county from membership, calling it “not a decision I made lightly.”
* **Cites concerns over transparency and internal decision-making:** Schleiker said his decision was driven by concerns about independence, lack of transparency, and being excluded from key meetings, adding that explanations he received from leadership did not match information from the Secretary of State’s office.
* **Raises broader questions about election governance:** He also questioned whether the association operates in a truly nonpartisan manner and warned that outside influence and limited input from clerks could undermine confidence in election-related decision-making.

* **Homeowner blocked from rebuilding single-family home:** A Lakewood resident who purchased a burned-out house to rehabilitate it was denied permission to rebuild a single-family home due to zoning changes, leaving the property an unusable eyesore.
* **Zoning rules prioritize higher-density development:** City planners told the owner the property must be redeveloped with multiple units—at least four under current rules—rather than a single home, reflecting broader policies shifting away from single-family housing.
* **Critics raise concerns about transparency and property rights:** The article highlights that zoning changes are not always clear to buyers and can render homes “non-conforming,” meaning they cannot be rebuilt after damage, fueling concerns about hidden regulations and loss of traditional property use.

| | | | High school dropout. Waffle House waitress. First woman to graduate from The Citadel. Single mom. Fighter.

Nancy Mace wasn’t born into power. She worked for every inch of ground she’s gained.

At 17, she dropped out of high school and took a job slinging hash browns at Waffle House to survive. No silver spoon. No Ivy League connections. Just grit, grace, and a whole lot of graveyard shifts.

By the grace of God, she turned that struggle into a story no politician can touch. She made history as the first woman to graduate from The Citadel, South Carolina’s legendary military college. She built her own business. She raised two kids on her own. And when the Left came for everything she believed in, she stood her ground. Now, she’s running for Governor of South Carolina.

Nancy Mace is a battle-tested conservative who’s walked through fire and come out swinging. In Congress, she’s been one of President Trump’s fiercest allies, fighting to secure our border, protect our daughters, and stop the Left’s sick agenda dead in its tracks.

She’s not here to make friends. She’s here to make history.

Nancy is fighting to:

* Eliminate South Carolina’s Income Tax—the highest in the Southeast

* Prosecute violent criminals and pedophiles with zero leniency

* Crack down on sanctuary sheriffs who let illegal aliens roam free

* Defund radical public universities that indoctrinate, not educate

* Reform education so students learn how to think—not what to think

* Work hand-in-hand with President Trump to put South Carolina FIRST

Through every hardship, Nancy never gave up. And now she’s ready to do what she’s always done: roll up her sleeves, take the heat, and lead from the front.

South Carolina is worth fighting for. And Nancy Mace is just getting started.

clean_body: | | | | | | | | Hi, This is Brigadier General James Emory Mace, U.S. Army (Retired). Today, I write to you not as a soldier... but as a father. I’m a Vietnam War Veteran and Purple Heart Medal recipient. I’ve worn the uniform. I’ve buried friends who never made it home. And I’ve felt the sting of a Nation that sometimes forgets what our sacrifices were for. But my daughter - Congresswoman Nancy Mace - never forgot. Nancy was raised in the shadow of the flag. She saw the uniform. She lived with the deployments. She knew the cost. And instead of running from it, she ran toward it. That’s the kind of person -the kind of fighter \- she is. When Nancy was 17, she dropped out of high school. Most kids in that situation fall apart. But not Nancy. I raised her to believe that setbacks don’t define you -how you rise does. She grew up hearing the same lessons over and over again: 👉 Never quit. 👉 Never run from the truth.👉 And never let anyone tell you thatyou are less than what God made you to be. So I gave her a choice: She picked herself up, took a job at Waffle House, and fought her way back. By 21, she became the first woman to graduate from The Citadel, following in my footsteps. Soon after, she was elected as the first woman to represent South Carolina in the U.S. House of Representatives. She’s been fighting her whole life; for herself, for her kids, for the truth, and now...for her state. Nancy led an evacuation mission in the Middle East after learning a South Carolina family was stranded. Because when your people are stuck in a war zone getting hit with missiles and rockets, the only answer worthy of the office -worthy of our country \- is to get them out. She flew into an active war zone and answered the call when Americans needed help. As a father - and as a Purple Heart Veteran \- I’ve never been more proud of my daughter. That’s why it’s hard when I have to watch Nancy face relentless attacks day after day. Each day that goes out there and fights for you, she’s up against the Establishment’s knife. They stalk her.
